description: Discipline focused on keeping systems dependable, minimizing downtime, protecting data, and restoring services after failures through reliability engineering, high availability, backups, and disaster recovery planning.

children.description: Metrics used to quantify service dependability, outage frequency, recovery performance, and operational risk.
Measures average operating time between repairable failures; higher values generally indicate greater reliability.
Measures average time required to restore service after a failure; lower values improve resilience.
Service commitments defining acceptable availability, latency, and error thresholds for users.
Availability concerns access to services; durability concerns long-term preservation of data.
Architectural approaches that keep services running despite component, infrastructure, or regional failures.
Techniques that duplicate critical resources to eliminate single points of failure.
Multiple live instances serve traffic simultaneously and share workload.
Standby resources remain ready and take over during failures.
Provides at least one extra component beyond normal capacity requirements.
Design patterns commonly used to improve uptime and graceful failure handling.
Distribute traffic across instances to improve availability and scalability.
Automatically redirect workloads to healthy resources during outages.
Maintains partial functionality when full service cannot be sustained.
Prevent cascading failures and improve recovery from transient issues.
Operational capabilities used to detect, respond to, and recover from failures.
Tracks infrastructure and application signals in real time.
Automatically detect and remediate common failures.
Uses automation to restart, replace, or recover failed components.
Practices for preserving recoverable copies of data and systems.
Different methods for capturing and storing recoverable data.
Creates a complete copy of protected data.
Stores only changes since the most recent backup.
Stores changes since the last full backup.
Operational guidelines that improve backup reliability and recoverability.
Keep three copies, on two media types, with one copy offsite.
Protects backup integrity and reduces ransomware risk.
Leverages managed cloud services for backup and protection.
Validates that backups can actually be recovered when needed.
Processes and architectures for restoring services and data after major disruptions.
Business-defined recovery targets that guide DR design.
Maximum acceptable downtime before service restoration is required.
Maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time.
Different readiness levels for disaster recovery environments.
Lowest-cost option with longer recovery times.
Partially prepared environment enabling faster restoration.
Continuously synchronized environment enabling near-immediate recovery.
Engineering and operational practices used to execute disaster recovery plans.
Managing latency, consistency, and coordination across regions.
Uses distributed consensus to maintain correctness during failures.
Redirects workloads between geographic regions during outages.
Controlled failure experiments that validate resilience and recovery.
